(1) THE FRANC IS THE WEAKEST CURRENCY ON THE BOARD, not the strongest: CHF is at a 13-month low vs USD and EUR/CHF has broken out to 0.9332 because the SNB's 0% is the widest rate disadvantage in the developed world and the Bank is actively talking the franc lower - USD/CHF and EUR/CHF flip from SHORT to LONG. (2) THE WAR PREMIUM IS DEFLATING AGAIN: the US held off the strikes Trump threatened for the weekend, Iran and Oman are negotiating Hormuz transit in Tehran, WTI is back to ~$83-84 from $86 and gold has slipped to ~$4,053 - USOIL flips to SHORT, XAU to RANGE. The yen is the one clean long: it HELD the intervention gains at ~157 and Tokyo July core CPI jumped to 1.9%. Also corrected: the RBNZ's next meeting is Sept 2, NOT Aug 19. Cleanest trades: CHF/JPY SHORT, AUD/JPY SHORT, EUR/CHF LONG, USD/JPY SHORT, JPYBASKET LONG. Next gate: US July jobs Fri Aug 7 (consensus +85k).

meta.regime: Risk premium is coming OUT of the market and the haven trade has split in two. On the geopolitics, the escalation Friday's tape promised did not happen: after Trump told a Cabinet meeting the US would be 'hitting them very hard' and fresh strikes were expected over the weekend, Washington forewent attacking, Trump said the US halted strikes at the Iranian regime's request, and Iranian and Omani deputy foreign ministers are meeting in Tehran on a compromise that would let Iran run Hormuz transit with fewer restrictions on ships. WTI has come off to roughly $83-84 from $86 with Brent near $85-88, gold has slipped to ~$4,053 from $4,086 and silver sits at $58.25. That deflates the CAD terms-of-trade bid, kills the USOIL long and takes gold off the long list. The bigger structural change is the franc: CHF is at a 13-month low against the dollar and EUR/CHF has broken out to 0.9332, because with the SNB at 0% the franc now carries the widest rate disadvantage in the developed world, the Bank is openly talking it lower, and markets are pricing a higher probability of two more ECB hikes this year. A haven that no longer catches a haven bid while its policy rate is pinned at zero is simply a funding currency - so every CHF cross inverts. The yen is the opposite case and the one unambiguous long: it HELD the MoF intervention gains near 157 rather than giving them back, the BoJ held 1.00% with Takata dissenting for a hike, and Tokyo July core CPI jumped to 1.9% from 1.6% with headline at 2.0%. The dollar had its worst week in three months (DXY -1.5%, monthly -1.3%) but bounced to 100.3 on Friday, and September hike pricing is still live at roughly 60% on prediction markets and up near 82% in fed funds futures.
meta.nextBigEvent: US July employment report (Fri Aug 7, 12:30Z). The Bloomberg consensus is +85k after June's +57k, with unemployment at 4.2% and April-May revised down 74k combined. A second sub-100k print kills the September hike the three FOMC dissenters (Hammack, Kashkari, Logan) are pushing and breaks the dollar lower; a clean beat re-arms it and would hit the EUR, GBP and JPY longs at once. July CPI on Aug 12 is the follow-up.

dailyRead: Two theses flipped overnight and both cut the same way - less fear in the price. Start with the franc, because it is the bigger structural change and it inverts a whole block of the book. CHF is trading at a 13-month low against the dollar and EUR/CHF has broken out to 0.9332, and the reason is not the war tape at all: with the SNB policy rate pinned at 0% the franc now carries the widest rate disadvantage in the developed world, Schlegel's committee is openly talking it lower rather than leaning against strength, and markets have moved to price a higher probability of two further ECB hikes this year. Friday's file had CHF as the strongest currency on the board on a 're-armed haven bid' - that read is wrong and the price action says so. USD/CHF and EUR/CHF flip from SHORT to LONG, GBP/CHF and NZD/CHF go LONG, and CHF/JPY becomes the cleanest short on the board because it pairs the weakest currency against the strongest. Second, the war premium is deflating again. Trump told a Cabinet meeting on Friday the US would be 'hitting them very hard' and fresh strikes were expected over the weekend; they did not come. Washington forewent attacking, Trump said the US halted strikes at the Iranian regime's request while warning they resume if no new ceasefire lands, and Iranian and Omani deputy foreign ministers are sitting in Tehran negotiating a compromise that would have Iran run Hormuz transit with fewer restrictions on ships. WTI has come back to roughly $83-84 from $86, Brent to about $85-88 from $91, gold has slipped to ~$4,053 from $4,086 and silver is $58.25. So USOIL flips from LONG to SHORT, XAU falls from LONG to RANGE, CAD loses the terms-of-trade leg that was its only bid (June CPI 2.8% with median core 1.9% and trim 1.8%, five-year lows, and a sixth BoC hold), and GER40 gets a genuine tailwind for the first time in weeks. The yen is the exception and the one unambiguous long: rather than giving back the MoF intervention as it did in April-May, it HELD near 157 against a 40-year low of 164, the BoJ held 1.00% with Hajime Takata dissenting FOR a hike and an Outlook Report that sees core inflation clearly above 2% from H2 FY26, and Tokyo July core CPI has now jumped to 1.9% from 1.6% with headline at 2.0% - a fresh, forward-looking confirmation that the BoJ's own forecast is being validated. Jobs-to-applicants also ticked back up to 1.18. On the dollar, the week was ugly - DXY fell about 1.5%, its worst week in three months, with a 1.3% monthly decline - but it bounced to 100.3 on Friday and September hike pricing is far from dead at roughly 60% on prediction markets and near 82% in fed funds futures, so lean short USD without pressing it into Friday's payrolls, where consensus is +85k. Elsewhere: sterling firmed on the BoE's hawkish 6-3 hold and TE now shows UK employment up 148k in May with wage growth 4.3% and unemployment down to 4.9%; the euro has the ECB two-hike pricing behind it even though annual growth is only 0.3%; Australia's June employment was actually strong at +76.3k with inflation expectations dropping to 4.7%, but the Q2 trimmed mean at 3.6% leaves August RBA hike odds at 4%; and New Zealand needs a correction - the RBNZ's next decision is Sept 2, NOT Aug 19 as Friday's file said, and the Bank's own July statement credited the partial Hormuz reopening with lowering oil and easing near-term inflation, so cheaper crude cools exactly the petrol-CPI engine that drove the 4.1% Q2 print. That is why AUD/NZD comes down from HIGH conviction to MED. Cleanest expressions today: CHF/JPY SHORT and AUD/JPY SHORT (weakest legs against the strongest), EUR/CHF LONG, USD/JPY SHORT and JPYBASKET LONG on a yen that held its defence, EUR/USD and GBP/USD LONG on the soft dollar, and USOIL SHORT on the deflating premium. The governing caveat cuts both ways now: these talks have collapsed twice already, and a breakdown in Tehran would snap oil, gold and the franc's crosses back within a session - while a second MoF strike would spike the yen further and reward every yen short already on.

today.headline: THESIS FLIP - the franc is at a 13-month low against the dollar and EUR/CHF has broken out to 0.9332, driven by the SNB's 0% policy rate being the widest rate disadvantage in the developed world while markets price two more ECB hikes this year.
today.read: Stop treating CHF as a haven and start treating it as a funding currency: with the war premium deflating there is no bid to offset a zero policy rate, and the SNB is actively talking the franc lower rather than leaning against strength. USD/CHF and EUR/CHF flip from SHORT to LONG, GBP/CHF and NZD/CHF go LONG, and CHF/JPY becomes the highest-conviction short on the board. Risk: a collapse in the Tehran talks restores the haven bid fast, and the SNB has said it would sell francs against rapid appreciation if it had to.

today.read: CAD loses the only leg it had. Domestically it is dovish - June CPI 2.8% with median core 1.9% and trim 1.8%, five-year lows, and a sixth straight BoC hold at 2.25% - so without a crude premium there is nothing to buy. USD/CAD comes off SHORT to RANGE, CAD/JPY flips to SHORT, and USOIL flips to SHORT. Risk: these talks have collapsed twice already; a breakdown snaps crude and CAD back in a session.

today.headline: Markets have moved to price a higher probability of TWO further ECB hikes this year against a deposit rate held at 2.25% - the mechanical driver behind the EUR/CHF breakout to 0.9332.
today.read: EUR is the natural long against the zero-rate franc, and it holds up against a soft dollar and a hike-free AUD. But the thesis has a hole: euro-area annual growth is 0.3%, HICP has already cooled to 2.8% with core 2.4%, and cheaper crude deflates the energy-inflation argument the hawks lean on - so cap EUR/USD conviction at MED and put the conviction into EUR/CHF instead. Risk: a dovish ECB tone on Sept 11, or a hot US CPI on Aug 12.

USD.note: Held 9-3 at 3.50-3.75% on Jul 29 with Hammack, Kashkari and Logan dissenting FOR a hike and no forward guidance from Chair Warsh. Q2 GDP 1.5%, June payrolls +57k and June PCE cooling to 3.7%/3.3% core argue against; the dissents and firm oil-led inflation argue for. July jobs (Aug 7, consensus +85k) and July CPI (Aug 12) decide it.

EUR.note: Held Jul 23 at 2.25% deposit facility. HICP 2.8% with core 2.4% and services 3.2%; markets have moved to price a higher probability of TWO further ECB hikes this year, which is the mechanical driver behind the EUR/CHF breakout. GDP annual growth of just 0.3% is the counterargument.

GBP.note: Held 3.75% on Jul 30 but 6-3, a third member joining Greene and Pill in dissenting for a hike. June CPI 2.6% with core 2.6% and services 3.6%, but TE now shows employment up 148k in May, wage growth 4.3% and unemployment down to 4.9% - a firmer labour market than the pause assumes.

JPY.note: Held 1.00% but Takata dissented FOR a hike; the Outlook Report upgraded FY26 GDP to ~0.8% and sees core inflation clearly above 2% from H2 FY26. Tokyo July core CPI has since jumped to 1.9% from 1.6% - the forecast is being validated in real time. MoF is defending spot in parallel and the defence has held.

AUD.note: Q2 trimmed mean MISSED at 3.6% (vs 3.7% exp) and the market prices only a 4% chance of an August hike. But June employment was strong at +76.3k, services PMI is 53.0 and inflation expectations dropped to 4.7% from 5.5% - a pause-and-observe hold with the labour market doing better than the CPI.

NZD.note: The RBNZ hiked 25bp to 2.50% on Jul 8, the first hike in three years, and said further increases remain possible with the pace data-dependent; TE's model has 2.75% by end-quarter. Note the Bank explicitly credited the partial Hormuz reopening with lowering oil and easing near-term inflation, and sees headline falling to ~2% over 12 months.

CAD.note: Held 2.25% on Jul 29 for a sixth straight time. June CPI cooled to 2.8% with median core 1.9% and trim 1.8% - five-year lows - so there is no rates leg at all, and with crude deflating the terms-of-trade leg is going too.

CHF.note: At ZERO, and Bloomberg-surveyed panellists see it there until 2027. June CPI 0.5% y/y with 0.0% m/m and core just 0.3%; producer and import prices are outright deflating at -2.1%. The SNB says it would sell francs against rapid appreciation but calls that unnecessary now - it is content to let the franc slide.

Layer on a central bank whose Outlook Report already forecasts core inflation clearly above 2% from H2 FY26 and a fresh Tokyo print moving exactly that way, and Oct/Dec becomes genuinely live; a Reuters poll has 70% of economists at 1.50%+ by Q2 2027. Every XXX/JPY cross is a short. Risk: a payrolls beat on Aug 7 re-pins USD/JPY higher, and a collapse in the Tehran talks would put the oil-importer drag straight back on.

catalysts.event: Iran/US - strikes paused again; Iran-Oman Hormuz transit talks in Tehran
catalysts.note: The escalation Friday promised did not arrive. Trump told a Cabinet meeting the US would be hitting Iran very hard and fresh strikes were expected over the weekend; Washington forewent attacking, with Trump saying the US halted at the Iranian regime's request while warning strikes resume if no new ceasefire lands. Iranian and Omani deputy foreign ministers are meeting in Tehran on a compromise that would let Iran run Hormuz transit with fewer restrictions on ships; Iran says it has no talks with the US itself. Traffic is still under 10 commodity ships a day against ~100 prewar. This has collapsed twice before - it is the two-way swing factor over oil, gold, CAD and the whole CHF block.

catalysts.event: MoF intervention watch - the defence has HELD so far
catalysts.note: Unlike the record 11.7trn yen April/May operation, which faded within six weeks, this one has stuck: spot is near 157 rather than back at the 164 forty-year low. That is what upgrades the yen from a spike to a regime. Authorities retain both the willingness and the precedent to strike again on any move back toward 164, so size yen shorts for a second operation in your favour and yen longs for a squeeze against you.

catalysts.event: New Zealand Q2 labour market report
catalysts.note: Unemployment was 5.3% in Q1 with employment +0.2% q/q. This is the next real input into whether the RBNZ follows July's hike on Sept 2, and the direct gate on AUD/NZD, NZD/JPY and NZD/CHF.

A second sub-100k print kills the September hike and breaks the dollar lower; a clean beat re-arms it and hits the EUR/USD, GBP/USD and USD/JPY positions simultaneously.

TE's models have the OCR at 2.75% by end-quarter after July's move to 2.50%. But the Bank credited the partial Hormuz reopening with lowering oil and easing near-term inflation and sees headline falling toward 2% - so cheaper crude between now and then argues for a pause.

Roughly 60% priced on prediction markets and near 82% in fed funds futures off the three July dissents from Hammack, Kashkari and Logan - but the July jobs and CPI prints stand between here and there.

Expected to hold at 0%, with Bloomberg-surveyed panellists seeing no change until 2027. The relevance is not the rate but the language: any hardening of the intervention pledge is the main cap on how far EUR/CHF and USD/CHF can run.

geopolitics: The premium is coming out of the price, but on a fragile basis. Friday's tape pointed one way - Trump told a Cabinet meeting the US would be hitting Iran very hard and fresh strikes were expected as soon as the weekend - and then the strikes did not come. Washington forewent attacking, at least for the near term, with Trump saying the US halted at the Iranian regime's request while warning that attacks resume if a new ceasefire deal is not reached, and diplomatic effort has concentrated on reopening the waterway. Iranian and Omani deputy foreign ministers are meeting in Tehran on a compromise that would allow Iran to run vessel transit through the Strait of Hormuz with fewer restrictions on ships, though Tehran maintains it has no negotiations with the United States itself. This is not a resolution: US and Saudi aircraft struck militia sites in Iraq after drones were launched toward Saudi Arabia, Foreign Minister Araghchi has warned Iran will respond forcefully to any further American aggression, the State Department has warned US citizens across the Middle East, and traffic through the strait is still under 10 commodity ships a day against roughly 100 on a normal prewar day, with about 27% of the world's seaborne crude and product trade normally passing through. FX transmission: (1) Crude is the transmission channel and it is falling - WTI back to roughly $83-84 from $86 and Brent to about $85-88 from $91 - so CAD loses the terms-of-trade bid that was its only support and USOIL flips from LONG to SHORT. (2) Gold slips to ~$4,053 from $4,086 and comes off the LONG list to RANGE; the soft-dollar leg survives, the war leg does not. Silver at $58.25 is the more balanced of the two because de-escalation and cheaper energy help its industrial leg even as the haven leg fades. (3) The franc is the biggest casualty and the most important trade: CHF only worked while the premium was expanding, and at a 13-month low against the dollar with the SNB pinned at 0% it is now a funding currency - LONG USD/CHF, EUR/CHF, GBP/CHF, NZD/CHF and AUD/CHF, SHORT CHF/JPY. (4) The yen is unaffected by this because its bid is domestic and official - a held MoF defence plus a hawkish BoJ - which is precisely why it is the one clean long. (5) GER40 gets a real energy-cost tailwind for the first time in weeks. (6) The whole book is one headline from inverting: these talks have collapsed twice already and Trump has explicitly conditioned the pause on a deal, so size the oil, gold and franc positions for a violent snap-back rather than a trend.
